chapter_title: Rama to the Rescue (Fables and Folk Tales)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 6 periods = 240 minutes
Total: 6 periods · 4h 0min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Comic-Strip Folk Tale Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.22): circle the odd one — characters and intruder.
Let us discuss (p.23): true or false — man's plan and thief's wish.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the comic-strip story aloud (pp.20–24), pausing at each panel while students follow the illustrations and dialogue. Students track who is speaking and what is happening in each frame.
Continue reading pp.24–27 aloud; at p.22 pause for "Let us discuss" — students circle the odd character and name who entered the house. Brief whole-class check on answers.
Students work in pairs on the true-or-false task (p.23) — judging whether the man shared his plan and whether the thief's wish came true. Pairs share verdicts; teacher consolidates with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The story is a Tamil Nadu folk tale presented as a comic strip, so character names and visual speech bubbles carry the plot — draw students' attention to the husband's whispered plan and the double meaning of the name 'Rama' as both a distress signal and the kotwal's actual name. A common pitfall is students treating the 'children' option as a real character rather than recognising it as the odd one out in a story where no children appear. Students who finish early may be directed to re-read the husband's whispered dialogue panels and note which words are printed smaller or softer.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension: Predict, Discuss, and Map the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.24): call 'Rama' softly/loudly; predict what happens next.
Let us discuss (p.26): fill story map — characters, setting, problem, solution.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.25): match words in Column A with meanings in Column B.

time_bands.activity: Students call out 'Rama' together — softly, then loudly, then very loudly — as the story instructs (p.24). Teacher briefly asks why volume matters in the husband's plan, drawing out the idea of the coded signal.
Class predicts aloud what will happen next, then teacher reads the story's resolution (pp.24–27) together with students, revealing how the kotwal heard his name and arrested the thief.

Students individually fill in the story-map boxes (p.26) — main characters, setting, other characters, problem, solution — then share with a partner. Teacher facilitates a brief whole-class comparison, consolidating the solution: the wife's coded calls brought the kotwal.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full story aloud together, students now have the complete narrative arc; the story-map task works best when students first agree on the problem before deciding the solution, so prompt the pair-share in that order. A common confusion is listing the kotwal as a 'main character' rather than an 'other character' — the couple's wit drives the plot; Rama is the instrument. For the vocabulary-matching task not covered in class, direct students to p.25 of the textbook as independent reading.

periods.activity_title: Analysing Extract and Listening for Safety Instructions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect II (p.27): answer three short questions on story events.
Let us listen (p.32): fill blanks while listening to security announcement.

time_bands.activity: Students answer the three short questions from "Let us think and reflect II" (p.27) — why the couple could not sleep, what the thief wished for, and how the couple got help — writing individually, then sharing with a partner. Teacher draws out the idea of coded communication as the central cleverness.

Teacher reads the security guard's neighbourhood announcement aloud twice at a steady pace (p.38 transcript). Students listen and fill the four blanks in the listening task (p.32) with the single words they hear.

Quick whole-class review of the four listening answers; teacher reads each sentence, students call out their answers, and the class agrees on the correct word for each blank. Any disagreement is resolved by reading the relevant sentence of the announcement again.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the story's events in detail, students are well placed to explain the couple's method in their own words — press them to use the phrase 'coded signal' or 'indirect call for help' rather than simply retelling the plot. For the listening task, read the announcement at a natural, unhurried pace; students often miss the emergency number (100) because it is at the end — a brief pause before re-reading the final sentence helps. The reflective question on cleverness (p.27, task index 6, question 4) is not anchored in class; students who wish to explore it may do so independently.

periods.activity_title: Speaking on Safety and Writing the Man's Account

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.33): discuss in pairs why safety matters and share three ideas.
Let us write (p.34): write narrative as the man, covering when, where, what, how, why.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models one or two contracted forms (I'm, it's, they're) spoken aloud, students repeat; this is a brief warm-up to the speaking task, not a separate lesson, and takes no more than a few natural exchanges.

Students work in pairs on the speaking task (p.33) — they discuss why keeping a house safe is important, tick suitable reasons, then share three ideas using the given hints in complete sentences. Teacher circulates, prompting students to use full sentences and not just read the printed hints.

Teacher reads the writing prompt aloud (p.34) and models the opening line on the board: "My wife and I were about to go to sleep last night when we heard someone…" The class brainstorms what details — when, where, what, how, why — the man would include, building a shared plan on the board.

Students write their first-person narrative independently, using the shared plan and the given opening line. Teacher circulates and responds to individual questions. At the closing signal, students underline one sentence they are most pleased with, ready to share if called upon.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking task on safety (p.33) is genuinely open — students may name reasons and ideas beyond the printed hints, and those contributions are valuable. For the writing task, the narrative covers the whole episode from the couple's perspective, so ensure students include both the clever signal (calling 'Rama') and the kotwal's arrival; a common gap is ending the story at the moment the wife called out, leaving the resolution unwritten. The contractions speaking drill (task index 0) is not addressed as a full in-class activity here; students may practise independently using p.33.

periods.activity_title: Contractions, Present Progressive Tense and Adverbs

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.27): write full words for contracted forms I'm, it's, they're.
Let us learn (p.28): identify that highlighted sentences describe actions going on now.
Let us learn (p.29): fill blanks using present progressive tense.
Let us learn (p.30): complete adverb table from story sentences — closely, softly, loudly.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.28): expand contracted words and write sentences for I'll, I'd, we'll, that's, we're, don't, you'll.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the three contracted lines from the story on the board (I'm, it's, they're) and asks students what letter is missing; students write the full forms. The link to the couple's whispered dialogue in the story grounds the concept in a familiar moment.

Teacher reads the five highlighted sentences from the story (p.28) aloud and asks: are these actions happening now, in the past, or in the future? Students choose the correct option (p.28, MCQ), then fill the six present-progressive blanks on p.29 individually.

Students turn to the adverb table on p.30, reading the three sentences from the story (closely, softly, very loudly) and completing the 'word' column. Teacher facilitates a brief class discussion on what an adverb tells the reader about a verb.

Quick whole-class review of the adverb table answers. Teacher introduces the homework task — expanding contracted words and writing their own sentences (p.28) — explaining the expansion pattern using 'what's = what is' as the model from the textbook.

periods.teacher_notes: All three grammar concepts (contractions, present progressive tense, adverbs of manner) appear in the story's own dialogue, so refer back to specific lines — the husband's whispered 'I'm feeling so sleepy' and the wife's 'I'll call out softly' — to make the grammar feel purposeful rather than abstract. A common error with the present progressive is students writing 'is sitting' instead of the correct form, particularly for the teachers in the staff room (p.29, blank 5); alert them to subject-verb agreement with plural subjects. Tasks on adverbs with picture-based fill-ins and exclamatory and interrogative sentences (pp.29–32) are not addressed in class and are available as self-study in the textbook.

periods.activity_title: Emergency Preparedness: Who Do You Call?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.34): find out and record who to call in six emergency situations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects the story's central act — calling for help cleverly — to real-life emergencies. Students brainstorm: what would you do if you saw a fire, or found a wounded animal? Record a few responses on the board to activate prior knowledge.

Students work in small groups to discuss the six situations from p.34 (fire, someone getting hurt, wounded animal, suspicious person, lost child, getting lost) and note down who they would call and what number, drawing on what they know and what they heard in the security announcement. Teacher circulates, prompting with questions about local emergency services.

Groups share their answers in a quick round; teacher records the agreed responses on the board, filling any gaps — especially the dial-100 reminder from the listening task. Students finalise their own written notes.

Teacher closes the unit by inviting students to name one thing the couple in the story and a real-life emergency caller have in common: staying calm and getting help without making the situation worse.

periods.teacher_notes: The story's theme of using wit to summon help provides a natural bridge to discussing real-world emergency responses; encourage students to name the actual numbers (100 for police, 101 for fire, 108 for ambulance) that are appropriate to their locality, which the security announcement introduced. A common gap is students naming only 'police' for every situation — push them to distinguish between fire, medical, and animal-welfare responses. The maze activity (p.35) is a light, enjoyable task students may attempt independently at home.
materials: List of local emergency numbers (if available)

items.source_lo: Student identifies characters, events and solutions by reading a folk-tale narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Husband-wife coded signal using kotwal's name 'Rama' to thwart a night-time thief.
items.item_stem: In the story, the husband whispers a plan to his wife so the thief cannot understand what they are doing. Which of the following best describes what the husband's plan involves?

options.label: A
options.text: Calling out the name of their unborn child at different volumes as a signal to the village kotwal.

options.label: B
options.text: Hiding their money under the floorboards before the thief could find it.

options.label: C
options.text: Pretending to be asleep so the thief would leave without taking anything.

options.label: D
options.text: Shouting for help directly at the top of their voices so that neighbours would hear them.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have confused the plan with a simple cry for help, missing the coded nature of the signal.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have misread the couple's quiet whispering as passive inaction rather than active deception.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student invents a detail not present in the story, suggesting a loose grasp of the narrative's actual events.

items.source_lo: Student identifies characters, events and solutions by reading a folk-tale narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Husband-wife coded signal using kotwal's name 'Rama' to thwart a night-time thief.
items.item_stem: The story shows that the couple solved their problem through cleverness rather than direct confrontation. Explain how the wife's actions led to the thief being caught. What does this tell you about the value the story places on quick thinking?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The wife called out the name 'Rama' at increasing volumes as agreed with her husband; when she called very loudly, Rama the kotwal — who was on patrol — heard his name, came to the house, and discovered and arrested the thief. The story suggests that quick wit and a calm, coded plan can be more effective than openly confronting danger.

items.source_lo: Student extracts specific information by listening to a public announcement as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Security guard's neighbourhood announcement: robbery alert, safety instructions, emergency number 100.
items.item_stem: Listen to the security guard's announcement being read aloud. Then decide whether each of the following statements is True or False.

options.text: Children are advised to report anything suspicious directly to the police.
The announcement says it is safe to accept items from strangers.
The emergency number mentioned in the announcement is 100.
The security guard says there have been reports of robbery in the locality.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the announcement opens with reports of robbery in the locality.
2. False — children are told to inform adults immediately, not to contact the police directly.
3. True — the announcement ends with 'Dial 100 in case of emergency.'
4. False — the announcement explicitly says not to talk to strangers or accept anything from them.

items.item_stem: The security guard's announcement gives different instructions to different groups of people. After listening, fill in the table below with the correct word or phrase for each blank.

Who is addressed | What they are instructed to do

Children | Inform 2. ____________ immediately about any suspicious activity.
Everyone | Do not talk to 3. ____________ or accept anything from them.
Anyone in an emergency | Dial 4. ____________ for immediate help.

items.item_stem: With a partner, take turns to describe two reasons why keeping your home safe is important. Use complete sentences. You may draw on what you know about the couple in the story and their experience with the thief.

expected_elements: States at least two reasons in complete sentences.
Connects at least one reason to the story's events.
Speaks clearly enough for a partner to follow.
Listens while the partner speaks without interrupting.

items.source_lo: Student expresses and justifies opinions in paired conversation using a narrative's theme as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Importance of household safety; three ideas for keeping home and self safe.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are advising a friend whose family has just moved into a new house. Share three ideas for keeping the house and family safe, giving a reason for each idea. You may take the role of the man from the story who has just had a frightening experience, or speak as yourself.

expected_elements: Offers three distinct safety ideas, not repetitions.
Gives a reason or justification for each idea.
Uses a register appropriate for advising a friend.
Maintains a clear, audible speaking pace throughout.

items.source_lo: Student writes a first-person narrative recounting events using a folk tale as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Man retells the night's events to a neighbour: coded plan, wife's calls, kotwal's arrival.
items.item_stem: You are the man from the story. Your neighbour has just knocked on your door the morning after the incident. Write a short account (five to six sentences) telling your neighbour what happened, using the points: when it happened, where the thief got in, what plan you made with your wife, how the kotwal was called, and what happened to the thief in the end.

expected_elements: Writes in first person throughout the account.
Includes the five key points: when, where, plan, signal, outcome.
Uses past tense consistently for the events.
Maintains a clear sequence of events from start to end.

items.source_lo: Student writes a first-person narrative recounting events using a folk tale as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Man retells the night's events to a neighbour: coded plan, wife's calls, kotwal's arrival.
items.item_stem: The man and his wife used quick thinking to stay safe. Write a paragraph (six to eight sentences) from the wife's point of view, describing the same night's events. Include what she noticed, what she felt when her husband whispered the plan, and why she thinks their cleverness was the most important part of the whole episode.

expected_elements: Adopts the wife's first-person voice consistently.
Includes her observation of the break-in and her feelings.
Explains the plan and the wife's role in executing it.
Offers a personal opinion on why cleverness mattered, in her voice.

items.source_lo: Student recognises and applies contractions, present progressive tense and adverbs of manner using a narrative's language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Contractions (I'm, it's, they're), present progressive tense, adverbs of manner (closely, softly, loudly) from story dialogue.
items.item_stem:
Read the following sentences from the story. Rewrite each sentence by (a) changing the verb in brackets to the present progressive tense and (b) adding a suitable adverb of manner from the box to describe how the action is done. Adverbs: softly, closely, quickly, loudly.
1. The husband (listen) to every sound in the house.
2. The wife (call) the name so the kotwal will hear.
3. The thief (move) through the hole he has dug.
4. Rama the kotwal (run) towards the house.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable answers follow the pattern 'is/are + verb-ing + adverb'; for example: 1. The husband is listening closely to every sound in the house. 2. The wife is calling loudly so the kotwal will hear. 3. The thief is moving softly through the hole he has dug. 4. Rama the kotwal is running quickly towards the house. Adverb choices may vary as long as they are drawn from the box and make logical sense with the sentence.

items.source_lo: Student connects a narrative's theme to real-world civic responsibility by researching emergency responses as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Six emergency situations: fire, injury, wounded animal, suspicious person, lost child, getting lost.
items.item_stem:
In the story, the couple found a clever way to call for help. In real life, different emergencies need different responses. Choose any three of the six situations below and, for each one, write: (a) who you would call or where you would go for help, and (b) one thing you should NOT do in that situation.
Situations: you see a fire; you see someone getting hurt; you see a wounded animal; you notice someone acting suspiciously; you find a lost child; you yourself get lost.

expected_elements: Addresses all three chosen situations with both parts (a) and (b).
Names a specific, realistic contact or authority for each situation.
Identifies a sensible 'do not do' action showing awareness of safety.
Writes in clear sentences appropriate for a real-world context.

items.source_lo: Student connects a narrative's theme to real-world civic responsibility by researching emergency responses as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Six emergency situations: fire, injury, wounded animal, suspicious person, lost child, getting lost.
items.item_stem: Design a small 'Emergency Contacts Chart' that a family could keep at home. Your chart must: (a) list at least four different emergency situations from the story's theme of safety, (b) name the correct person or number to call for each, (c) include one short safety tip for each situation, and (d) be set out clearly so any member of the family can read it quickly in a crisis. Write a brief note (two to three sentences) below the chart explaining why you chose to present the information the way you did.

expected_elements: Chart lists four or more distinct emergency situations.
Correct contact or number is given for each situation.
Each entry includes one practical, relevant safety tip.
Brief note explains the design choice with a clear reason.
